title: Views & Surface Area — Homework
intro: The six homework questions: views, volume and surface area. Do each on paper first, then check here — and play with the lab that unlocks after you solve it.

questions.title: Views of a Stack
questions.text: The numbers show how many cubes are stacked on each square of the base (**BACK** at the top of the plan, **FRONT** at the bottom). Do the drawings on paper first: the **FRONT view** and the **RIGHT view** (front row on the left). Then pick the line that has both views right **and** the number of cubes in all.
hints: FRONT view: stand at the front. In each **column** of the plan only the tallest stack shows.

Columns, left to right: (1, 2, 0), (3, 1, 2), (0, 2, 1) → the tallest in each. For the RIGHT view use each **row**, starting with the **front** row (the bottom row of the plan): 0 2 1, then 2 1 2, then 1 3 0.
Front view **2, 3, 2**. Right view **2, 2, 3**. For the number of cubes, add all nine numbers in the plan.

traps.0: This right view reads the rows from the **back** row first. Looking from the right side, the **front** row is on your left, so start with the front row (0 2 1 → 2).
traps.2: 9 is the number of **squares** in the base. The numbers are stack heights — add them: 1 + 3 + 0 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 1.
traps.3: Here the front view was built from the **rows** and the right view from the **columns**. The other way round: FRONT = tallest in each column, RIGHT = tallest in each row.

solution: FRONT view (tallest in each column, left to right): column 1 → 2, column 2 → 3, column 3 → 2. So **2, 3, 2**.
RIGHT view (tallest in each row, front row first): front row → 2, middle row → 2, back row → 3. So **2, 2, 3**.
Cubes in all: 1 + 3 + 0 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 1 = **12** → second line.
questions.idea: Front = tallest of each column. Right = tallest of each row, front row first. Cubes = add the plan.

questions.title: Half the Edges
questions.text: A larger cube has volume 64 cm³. A smaller cube has edges that are **half** the length of the edges of the larger cube. What is the volume of the smaller cube?
hints: Start with the larger cube: which number multiplied by itself three times makes 64?
The larger edge is 4 cm. Half of it is 2 cm.

traps.3: 16 is 64 ÷ 4 — that is what happens to an **area** when the edges are halved (two lengths halve). A volume has **three** lengths, so it is divided by 2 three times.

solution: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so the larger edge is **4 cm**.
Half of 4 is **2 cm**, so the volume is 2 × 2 × 2 = **8 cm³**.
Shortcut: every edge × ½ means volume × ½ × ½ × ½ = × ⅛, and 64 ÷ 8 = 8.
questions.idea: Edges × k → area × k², volume × k³.

questions.title: A Missing Edge
questions.text: The volume of the rectangular prism shown is 60 cm³. What is the value of *x*?
hints: Volume of a box = length × width × height. The three lengths are 4, 5 and *x*.
20 × *x* = 60. What do you multiply 20 by to get 60?

traps.0: Check it: if *x* were 1, the volume would be 4 × 5 × 1 = 20 cm³, not 60.
traps.1: Check it: if *x* were 4, the volume would be 4 × 5 × 4 = 80 cm³, not 60.
traps.2: Check it: if *x* were 6, the volume would be 4 × 5 × 6 = 120 cm³, not 60.
traps.4: Check it: if *x* were 2, the volume would be 4 × 5 × 2 = 40 cm³, not 60.

questions.idea: Volume = l × w × h — divide to find the missing length.

questions.title: A Corner Removed
questions.text: A 3 × 3 × 3 cube is built from 27 small cubes with edge 1 cm. **One corner cube is removed**, as shown. What is the surface area of the new solid?

explorer.extra: Full cube: 54. Take a corner away: **3 faces disappear** from the outside, but **3 new faces** show inside the notch — so the surface area stays the same. Try removing a second corner!

hints: First find the surface area of the **full** 3 × 3 × 3 cube: 6 faces, each 3 × 3.
The corner cube showed **3** of its faces on the outside. Those 3 squares are gone now.
But taking the cube away uncovers **3 new** squares inside the notch (the faces of the three neighbouring cubes that used to touch it). Gone 3, new 3 — what happens to the total?

traps.1: 51 = 54 − 3: you took away the 3 outside faces of the removed cube, but forgot the **3 new faces** inside the notch.
traps.3: 57 = 54 + 3: you counted the 3 new faces inside the notch, but forgot that the removed cube also took its **3 outside faces** away.

solution: Full cube: 6 × (3 × 3) = **54 cm²**.
Remove one corner cube: its 3 outside faces vanish (−3).
Its 3 neighbours now show a face inside the notch (+3).
54 − 3 + 3 = **54 cm²** — the same surface area, even though the solid lost a cube.
Check by gluing: 26 cubes × 6 = 156 faces; joints 54 − 3 = 51; 156 − 2 × 51 = 54 ✅
questions.idea: Surface area counts faces you can touch: lose 3, gain 3.

questions.title: Nine Digits, One Box
questions.text: The digits from 1 to 9 are each used exactly once to write three one-digit integers and three two-digit integers. The one-digit integers are equal to the length, width and height of a rectangular prism. The two-digit integers are equal to the areas of the faces of the same prism. What is the surface area of the rectangular prism?
hints: Surface area = 2 × (the three face areas), so first find the three side lengths (one-digit numbers).
Which digits **cannot** be a side? A side of **1** gives a one-digit area. A side of **5** gives areas ending in 5 or 0 — a second 5 repeats the digit, and 0 is not allowed.
Try the sides **3, 6 and 9**. Their face areas are 3 × 6, 3 × 9 and 6 × 9. Do the six numbers use every digit from 1 to 9 once?
solution: Digits used: 3, 6, 9, 1, 8, 2, 7, 5, 4 — every digit from 1 to 9, once each ✅.
(Trying every possible triple of sides on a computer shows this is the only box that works.)
questions.idea: Surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh). Use the digit rules to rule out sides.

questions.title: B over A
questions.text: An 8 × 8 × *n* rectangular prism is made up from 1 × 1 × 1 cubes. Suppose that *A* is the surface area of the prism and *B* is the **combined** surface area of the 1 × 1 × 1 cubes that make up the prism. What is the sum of the values of *n* for which [[B/A]] is an integer?
hints: Write *A* with *n*: the prism has two 8 × 8 squares and four 8 × *n* rectangles.
*B*: the prism has 8 × 8 × *n* = 64*n* little cubes, and each cube has surface area 6.
*A* = 128 + 32*n* and *B* = 384*n*. Divide both by 32: [[B/A]] = 12*n* ÷ (*n* + 4) = 12 − 48 ÷ (*n* + 4). When is 48 ÷ (*n* + 4) a whole number?
solution: That is a whole number exactly when *n* + 4 divides 48. Since *n* ≥ 1, *n* + 4 can be 6, 8, 12, 16, 24 or 48.
questions.idea: Write both areas with *n*, simplify the fraction, then ask which divisors work.
